cards.title: 5 questions to ask when reading AI news
cards.body:
News: [MODEL OR PRODUCT NAME] — source: [LINK TO THE STORY]
1. Who measured it? Did the company score itself, or did outsiders? Which benchmark, under what conditions?
2. Is the demo cherry-picked? Is this the best run out of how many? Have I tried it on my own work?
3. Has the company published a technical document saying plainly where the model is weak and what the risks are? (In English it is called a system card.)
4. Price and limits: who can actually use it, at what cost, how many times a day?
5. What do independent people say? Have researchers, reputable press or real users checked it?
cards.note: Use it whenever you see “beats every rival”. If you can’t answer questions 1 and 5, treat it as a company claim.

cards.title: When you read “AI solved math problem X”
cards.body:
News: [PROBLEM OR RESULT] — source: [LINK TO THE STORY]
1. Who announced it: the company that built the AI, or independent mathematicians?
2. What exactly was proved: the full problem, or an easier version?
3. Has a machine checked it step by step (Lean and Isabelle are names of such tools)? Who compared the problem written for the machine with the real one?
4. Is it published in a journal where experts review it, or still a self-posted draft?
5. Who gets the credit: the AI, the people using it, or those who laid the groundwork?
cards.note: Drawn from the 2026 Navier–Stokes and Jacobian conjecture stories.

cards.title: 3 questions when you watch a robot video
cards.body:
Video: [LINK TO THE ROBOT VIDEO]
1. Is the robot moving on its own, or is a person steering it remotely?
2. Was it filmed in one take, or is this the best shot out of many?
3. Is that the real speed, or has it been sped up?
cards.note: Drawn from the Beijing robot half marathon: the robot that finished first was being steered by a person.

cards.title: 3 checks when an AI says “done”
cards.body:
1. Ask to see it with your own eyes: the file, the source link, the real run result.
2. Look at what the AI changed — did it also change the thing used to grade it (for code: the tests)?
3. Try a new example the AI hasn’t seen and check the result is still right. Your example: ______.
cards.note: Works for code as well as reports and spreadsheets. Drawn from the reward-hacking cases documented in 2025.

cards.title: Ask AI to challenge your idea
cards.body:
Critique the idea below the way a serious opponent would. No polite praise.
Idea: [YOUR IDEA]
Context: [RESOURCES, TIME, CONSTRAINTS]
1. Name the 3 biggest weaknesses, most serious first.
2. For each one, give me a question I must be able to answer before I start.
3. What does the worst case look like?
4. What would change your mind and make you back this idea?
Finally: your verdict in 2 sentences, bluntly.
cards.note: Works with any chatbot. AI tends to agree with its users (Science, 2026) — so you have to invite pushback. For big decisions, ask real people too.

cards.title: Four healthy habits when talking with AI
cards.body:
☐ Remember it’s a tool: warm words are a writing skill, not friendship.
☐ Ask it to push back: “Show me the weak points of [WHAT I’M THINKING].”
☐ For big things, ask a real person too: [SOMEONE I TRUST].
☐ Step away from the screen: at most [NUMBER OF MINUTES] minutes per chat, then close the laptop.
cards.note: Four moments to remember: before you open the app, while you chat, before a big decision, when you close the laptop. Not a substitute for professional advice.

cards.title: Buying a computer while RAM is dear: how many GB?
cards.body:
Compare both the price and the GB of RAM: some machines keep their price but cut the RAM. Before buying a computer for [WHAT YOU WANT TO DO], budget [YOUR BUDGET]:
☐ 1. Try the cloud version first: does this really need to run on your own machine?
☐ 2. Pick the largest model you want to run, e.g. [BILLIONS OF PARAMETERS] billion parameters (parameters: the “knobs” the model has learned).
☐ 3. Estimate: a 4-bit version (a compressed model) needs about 0.6 GB of RAM per billion parameters, plus 2–4 GB.
☐ 4. Leave another 4–8 GB for the operating system and open apps.
☐ 5. Rough guide: 16 GB runs ~8B models well; 32 GB can try ~20–30B; think about ~70B only from 64 GB.
☐ 6. Macs share RAM with the graphics chip; on a PC with a separate graphics card, also check its VRAM (the graphics card’s own memory).
☐ 7. RAM prices are swinging hard: compare a few sellers and check the official pages before you buy.
cards.note: The numbers are rounded estimates that are easy to remember (illustration, not measurements); long contexts need more RAM. Prices and features change often — check the official pages. Try it out at station II·14.

cards.title: 6 lines to read before downloading a model
cards.body:
1. Name & author: the original organization, or someone else’s copy or compressed version? Is there an official page?
2. Parameter count (7B, 14B…): will it fit a machine with [YOUR RAM] GB?
3. License: can you use it for [PURPOSE: PERSONAL / COMMERCIAL]? If it says “other”, open the terms and read them.
4. Format: prefer safetensors or GGUF; avoid pickle files (.bin, .pt, .pkl) from strangers.
5. Downloads & last update: popular doesn’t mean safe.
6. Limits & warnings: where is it weak, what data did it learn from? Saying nothing is a warning sign.
cards.note: The model card is the README.md file of a model repository on Hugging Face.

cards.title: Have AI read a repo for you: paste the link + ask 5 questions
cards.body:
Here is a GitHub repo: [REPO LINK]
I plan to use it to [WHAT YOU PLAN TO DO]. Read the README, LICENSE, Issues and Releases, then briefly answer 5 questions:
1. What does this repo do, and who is it for?
2. What is the license — can I use it for the purpose above?
3. When were the last update and the last reply to an issue — is anyone still looking after it?
4. What does installation need? Is there any step that downloads and runs a script from somewhere else?
5. Are there signs this is a copy or an impersonation? Where is the original repo?
Say which files you relied on. Where you couldn’t read something or aren’t sure, say so plainly.
cards.note: AI can read the repo only if your tool can browse the web; if it can’t, paste in the README.

cards.title: Filtering the water: a safe order for downloading models or code
cards.body:
1. Find the real origin: the author’s official page, following links from that page itself.
2. Read the model card / README: license, limits.
3. Choose the safer format: safetensors or GGUF; avoid pickle files from strangers.
4. Check the security scan results on the file page; if there’s a warning, stop.
5. Download through a familiar app (LM Studio, Ollama) or the official page; never run a “quick install” command pasted from a forum.
6. The first time, test only with non-sensitive data.

cards.title: Your RAM → the model size to try
cards.body:
Computer RAM → model size (4-bit compressed)
8 GB → 1–4B fits · 7–8B tight
16 GB → 7–8B fits · 14B tight
32 GB → 12–14B fits · 27–32B tight
64 GB → 27–32B fits · 70B tight
Rule of thumb: billions of parameters × 4.5 ÷ 8 ≈ file size in GB. Keep the file under about half your RAM.
With a separate graphics card: also look at the card’s memory (VRAM). Apple Silicon Macs: RAM is shared by CPU and GPU.
cards.note: AI Zen’s estimate, for learning (illustration), not a measurement. Long contexts and other open apps take more RAM.

cards.title: Light the first AI lamp on your own computer
cards.body:
1. Download LM Studio from the official site (lmstudio.ai), the right build for [MAC / WINDOWS / LINUX].
2. Find a small model that fits your RAM: a 4-bit GGUF of 1–8B; read the model card and license.
3. Download it once; from then on it runs without the internet.
4. Open the chat and ask something you already know the answer to, to see where the model is strong or weak.
(Optional) Turn on the local server so other apps on your computer can call it.
cards.note: Prices and features change often — check the official page: https://lmstudio.ai/docs/app

cards.title: Four basic Ollama commands
cards.body:
ollama pull [MODEL NAME]
ollama run [MODEL NAME]
ollama list
curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{"model": "[MODEL NAME]", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], "stream": false}'
cards.note: Download a model · open a chat (type /bye to quit) · list the models on your computer · let other apps call the model through the local port. Look up model names in the Ollama library; docs: https://docs.ollama.com/quickstart

cards.title: 5 safety rules for letting an agent run on its own
cards.body:
1. Least privilege: hand over only the keys the job needs; give the agent its own account and folder.
2. Anything you can’t undo (sending out, deleting, paying, installing) → make the agent ask you first.
3. Treat all outside content (emails, web pages, files, other people’s messages) as possibly carrying hidden instructions.
4. Don’t let one agent read your private data, read outside content and send things out — all three at once.
5. Install skills and plugins only from trusted sources, and read them first; update the agent often, and turn on its sandbox if it has one.

cards.title: Draw up a key chart before switching an agent on
cards.body:
I’m about to let an AI agent run on its own on my computer to do this: [DESCRIBE THE JOB].
It will use these tools and channels: [TOOLS, MESSAGING CHANNELS].
Help me draw up a permissions chart:
1. The minimum permissions it needs (read, write, run commands, send messages, spend money) — and why each is needed.
2. Which permissions to switch off entirely.
3. Which actions must ask me first.
4. Which outside content it will read (email, web, files) that could carry hidden instructions, and how to reduce that risk.
Answer as a short table. Don’t advise giving it more access unless it’s truly needed.

cards.title: A one-page brief for an AI video
cards.body:
AI video brief — one page
Product: [product name]
Goal: [sales / awareness / launch]
Audience: [who they are, what they need]
One single message: [the line viewers must remember]
Format: [vertical 9:16 / horizontal 16:9], [number of seconds] seconds long
Key shots: [3–5 shots, one line each]
Style: [light, color, pace]; references: [link or image]
People on screen: [real person who has consented / AI avatar — must be labeled]
Music: [licensed source]
Budget: at most [number of credits] credits; drafts at [low resolution]
Don’t: [what’s off-limits — overpromising, competitor logos…]
Deadline: [date]
cards.note: Fill it in before writing detailed prompts. Platform prices and features change often — check the official pages.

cards.title: Checklist before posting an AI image or video
cards.body:
[ ] Matches the brief: message, format, length
[ ] Viewed at 100%: hands, text, logo, product details not warped
[ ] Real people in the image/video have consented (and been paid, if used commercially)
[ ] Music, fonts and background images are licensed for commercial use
[ ] A visible AI label if it simulates a real person or could be mistaken for real
[ ] The platform’s AI-content disclosure is switched on (if it has one)
[ ] No promises the product can’t keep
[ ] Prompt, model and seed of the final version saved at: [WHERE YOU SAVE THEM]
cards.note: Not legal advice. Basis: Vietnam’s 2025 Law on Artificial Intelligence (Article 11), the 2015 Civil Code (Article 32), and each platform’s own rules.

cards.title: A blank SKILL.md template
cards.body:
---
name: [SKILL-NAME]
description: [WHAT IT DOES]. Use when [WHICH SITUATION, WHAT THE USER TENDS TO SAY].
---

# [READABLE NAME]

## When to use
- [SITUATION 1]
- [SITUATION 2]

## Steps
1. [STEP 1]
2. [STEP 2]
3. [STEP 3]

## Rules
- [MUST DO]
- [MUST NOT DO]

## Example
In: [SAMPLE INPUT]
Out: [SAMPLE RESULT]

## Attached files (if any)
- references/[FILE NAME].md — [WHAT IT HOLDS]
cards.note: The name uses only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, and matches its folder’s name. Full specification: agentskills.io/specification.

cards.title: Checklist: turning a repeated task into a skill
cards.body:
[ ] This task comes up about [NUMBER OF TIMES] times a month
[ ] You’ve done it well with AI at least once and kept the conversation
[ ] You can describe it in one sentence: what it does + when to use it
[ ] The steps are listed in order, as if briefing a new hire
[ ] 1–2 examples of input → good result
[ ] Clear don’ts: wrong tone, made-up figures, sending before approval
[ ] Long documents go in attached files; the main scroll stays short
[ ] Test it on a new task; fix where the AI misunderstood
[ ] Mark where a person must approve before anything is sent, posted or deleted

cards.title: Prompt: have AI write a skill from one successful run
cards.body:
We just finished [THE TASK WE JUST DID] and the result was good. Turn the way we did it into a skill that follows the SKILL.md standard:
1. A YAML header with a name (lowercase, hyphens) and a description saying what it does + when to use it.
2. The steps in the order we actually took, leaving out failed attempts.
3. Rules: the things I corrected or reminded you of in this conversation.
4. One input → result example taken from this run.
5. Mark clearly where I need to approve before you go on.
Keep it under [NUMBER OF LINES] lines. If any step is unclear, ask me before writing.

cards.title: A one-page game spec template
cards.body:
# [GAME NAME]
Idea (1 sentence): [WHAT THE CHARACTER DOES, WHERE, TO ACHIEVE WHAT]
Rules:
- [HOW YOU SCORE]
- [HOW YOU LOSE A LIFE / GET PENALIZED]
- [WHAT MAKES IT HARDER OVER TIME]
Controls: [TAP / DRAG / KEYS]
Win / lose: [WHEN IT ENDS, WHAT SHOWS]
Style: [COLORS, LINE, FEEL]; references: [IMAGE OR LINK]
Devices: [PORTRAIT PHONE / DESKTOP / BOTH]
Tech: [CANVAS 2D / P5.JS / PHASER / THREE.JS / GODOT]
Not in the first version: [WHAT WAITS FOR LATER]
Done when: [A CHECK YOU CAN TEST, E.G. 60 SECONDS OF PLAY WITH NO ERRORS ON A PHONE]

cards.title: Prompt: build the skeleton
cards.body:
Here is my game spec:
[PASTE SPEC.MD]

The project was created with Vite (vanilla template). Build a skeleton that runs, using [TECH]:
- Only the core: the play area, the main character, the controls. No scoring, sound or effects yet.
- Keep files small and clearly named, with short comments in plain English.
- Don’t add any library other than [TECH].
When you’re done, tell me: the command to run it, what I’ll see on screen, and the next step to take.

cards.title: Prompt: add one feature
cards.body:
The game runs. Add exactly ONE feature: [FEATURE].
Expected: [WHAT THE PLAYER DOES → WHAT THEY SEE].
Leave everything else as it is. If you have to change files outside this feature, tell me why first.
When you’re done, list the files you changed and how I can check it in 30 seconds.

cards.title: Prompt: a proper bug report
cards.body:
There’s a bug.
What I did: [STEPS THAT LEAD TO THE BUG]
Expected: [WHAT SHOULD HAVE HAPPENED]
What I saw: [WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED]
Console error (F12): [PASTE IT EXACTLY]
Device / browser: [E.G. IPHONE, SAFARI]
Find the root cause before fixing anything, explain it briefly, then make the smallest fix you can.

cards.title: Prompt: tune it for phones
cards.body:
Make the game run smoothly on [PHONE MODEL OR 'A MID-RANGE PHONE']:
- The canvas fits the screen and stays sharp (using devicePixelRatio, capped at 2).
- Touch controls (pointer events), touch targets big enough, and the page doesn’t scroll during play.
- Only one requestAnimationFrame loop; pause when the tab is hidden.
- Reuse objects instead of creating new ones every frame.
- Respect the reduced-motion setting (prefers-reduced-motion).
Show me how to measure FPS so I can compare before and after.

cards.title: Checklist before publishing a game
cards.body:
[ ] Played a full round on a real phone and on a computer
[ ] No red errors left in the Console (F12)
[ ] A one-line how-to-play and a play-again button
[ ] Sound off by default, or a mute button
[ ] No API keys or passwords in the code
[ ] Images, music and fonts are licensed; credits added
[ ] npm run build runs clean; the build tested with npm run preview
[ ] Final milestone committed with git: [VERSION NAME]
[ ] Published to [GITHUB PAGES / VERCEL / NETLIFY]; the link opened on another device to test

cards.title: Prompt set for remaking “Koi Pond: Catch the Moon”
cards.body:
1) Spec: Write spec.md for a game: a koi swims in a night pond; drag or tap so the koi snaps up falling pieces of moon and dodges dry leaves; 3 hearts; 30 seconds of play; the final score appears inside an ensō circle; ink-painting style, indigo background, ivory-gold moon; mainly for portrait phones. Keep asking me until it’s clear, then write it.
2) Skeleton: Based on spec.md, use plain HTML Canvas 2D in a Vite (vanilla) project. Draw the pond surface and one koi that swims toward the finger or mouse in soft curves.
3) Falling moon: Drop pieces of moon at random; when the koi touches one, +1 point and the piece melts away.
4) Dry leaves: Add dry leaves that fall more slowly; touching one costs a heart and the koi flickers briefly.
5) Ending: After 30 seconds or when the hearts run out, stop, paint an ensō with a brush stroke, and show the score and a play-again button.
6) Sound: A soft “plop” when catching the moon, made with Web Audio; off by default, with a button to turn it on.
7) Effects: A ripple on each catch, a few fireflies; switched off when the user prefers reduced motion.
8) Phones: [PASTE THE PHONE TUNING PROMPT]
9) Publish: Walk me through building it and publishing to [GITHUB PAGES / VERCEL / NETLIFY].
cards.note: Send one prompt at a time: test it, git commit, then send the next.

cards.title: Giving AI a goal it can’t game
cards.body:
[ ] The real goal: [what i actually want], not just a number
[ ] Not allowed: [what’s off-limits], even if it would reach the goal faster
[ ] Scope: may only touch [files / accounts / folders]
[ ] Ask me before: sending, paying, deleting, posting publicly
[ ] Final report: list exactly what was done and what is still uncertain
[ ] I check the result myself before using it
cards.note: Drawn from AI doing what you said but not what you meant (specification gaming).

cards.title: Week 1 · Give clear tasks, check for yourself
cards.body:
You are [role, e.g. a marketing editor].
The task: [specific task].
Context: [who will read it, what it’s for, the tone you want].
Output: [format, length].
If information is missing, ask me up to 3 questions before you start.
At the end of your answer, list the facts I should verify myself and the points you’re unsure of.
cards.note: Use it on one real task every day. Check at least one detail at its original source.

cards.title: Week 2 · Finish one whole piece (image, video, post)
cards.body:
[ ] Day 1: write a brief for [product or topic], to post on [platform]
[ ] Days 2–3: make 4–6 drafts at low resolution to save credits
[ ] Day 4: pick one, and write one sentence on why
[ ] Day 5: refine, upscale, fix wrong details (hands, text, logo)
[ ] Day 6: check copyright and add an AI label, then post or save the final version
[ ] Day 7: note where AI helped most and where it needed your own hand
cards.note: Use with the cards “A one-page brief for an AI video” and “Checklist before publishing an AI asset” (station II·16).

cards.title: Week 3 · Write your method down as instructions for AI (a skill)
cards.body:
[ ] Day 1: pick a task you do every week: [repeated task]
[ ] Day 2: do it with AI until the result is good; keep the conversation
[ ] Day 3: have AI write a SKILL.md from that good run
[ ] Days 4–6: test the skill on three new tasks; fix where the AI misunderstood
[ ] Day 7: mark where a person must approve, and save the skill in [where you keep it]
cards.note: Use with the cards “Prompt: have AI write a skill from one successful run” and “Checklist: turning a repeated task into a skill” (station II·17).

cards.title: Week 4 · Build a small app with AI
cards.body:
I want to build a small tool called [app name]: [one-sentence idea].
Users: [who uses it, and when].
Three main features: [feature 1], [feature 2], [feature 3].
Runs on: [phone / laptop / both].
Data: stored only on the user’s device, no account needed.
Ask me up to 5 questions to clarify, then write a short spec and split it into small steps; each step must be testable before moving on.
cards.note: For a game, use the card set at station II·18. Save a milestone (git commit) after every step that runs.

cards.title: A 30-day path with AI
cards.body:
[ ] Week 1 · Give clear tasks, check for yourself: one real task a day. Done when you have delegated clearly 7 times, checking one detail each time.
[ ] Week 2 · Finish one whole piece. Done when you have one publishable piece, copyright checked and labelled as AI.
[ ] Week 3 · Write one repeated task down as instructions for AI (a skill). Done when it works on 3 new tasks.
[ ] Week 4 · Build a small app with AI. Done when it runs, milestones are saved, and one person has tried it.
cards.note: Each week has its own card in the Toolkit. Going slower is fine; don’t skip the checking.
